Question:
A production NLP system uses BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) to classify customer support tickets.
The model performs well during training and validation. However, after deployment, latency becomes too high when the ticket text is long.
Profiling shows that most of the latency comes from the self-attention layers. BERT uses standard full self-attention, where every token attends to every other token.

The team is considering replacing BERT with an architecture designed to handle long sequences more efficiently, such as Longformer or BigBird.

Which change would most directly address the computational bottleneck for long sequences?
A: Replace ReLU with GELU in BERT
B: Use an attention mechanism with reduced attention complexity, such as sparse/local attentionB.
C: Increase the number of Transformer layers
Explaination:
In standard Transformer self-attention, every token attends to every other token.

For a sequence of length n, the attention computation is roughly:

O(n²)

So if the ticket becomes longer, the attention cost grows rapidly.

For example:

512 tokens ? attention matrix ? 512 × 512
2,048 tokens ? ? 2,048 × 2,048
4,096 tokens ? ? 4,096 × 4,096

That's why long insurance complaints/ticket descriptions can create significant latency.

What is sparse/local attention?

Instead of allowing every token to attend to every other token, attention is restricted.

Full attention:

Token 1 ? Token 1,2,3,4,...,n

Local attention:

Token 1 ? nearby tokens only

For example, each token might attend only to a window of 128 neighboring tokens.
Sub Topics: self attention; sparse attention; local attention
